claim: Fucosylation genes display widespread association with resistance to targeted therapies across multiple cancer types.
source: Large-scale pharmacogenomics revealed that fucosylation genes display widespread association with resistance to these therapies.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacogenomics data analysis from GDSC and CCLE datasets showing correlations between fucosylation gene expression and drug resistance.

claim: Targeted kinase inhibitors distinctively induced core fucosylation of secreted proteins less than 60 kDa in cancer cell cultures, xenograft mouse models, and patients.
source: In cancer cell cultures, xenograft mouse models, and patients, targeted kinase inhibitors distinctively induced core fucosylation of secreted proteins less than 60 kDa.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from multiple model systems including cell cultures, mouse xenografts, and patient samples showing increased fucosylation of <60 kDa proteins.

claim: PON1 fucosylation is a critical component of the therapy-induced secretome.
source: Label-free proteomics of N-glycoproteomes identified fucosylation of the antioxidant PON1 as a critical component of the therapy-induced secretome (TIS).
evidence: The claim is supported by label-free proteomics analysis identifying PON1 as a fucosylated component of the TIS.

claim: N-glycosylation of TIS and target core fucosylation of PON1 are mediated by the fucose salvage-FUT8-SLC35C1 axis.
source: N-glycosylation of TIS and target core fucosylation of PON1 are mediated by the fucose salvage-FUT8-SLC35C1 axis with PON3 directly modulating GDP-Fuc transfer on PON1 scaffolds.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the involvement of fucose salvage pathway, FUT8, and SLC35C1 in PON1 fucosylation.

claim: PON3 directly modulates GDP-Fuc transfer on PON1 scaffolds.
source: N-glycosylation of TIS and target core fucosylation of PON1 are mediated by the fucose salvage-FUT8-SLC35C1 axis with PON3 directly modulating GDP-Fuc transfer on PON1 scaffolds.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing PON3's role in regulating PON1 fucosylation.

claim: Core fucosylation in the Golgi impacts PON1 stability and folding prior to secretion, promoting a more degradation-resistant PON1.
source: Core fucosylation in the Golgi impacts PON1 stability and folding prior to secretion, promoting a more degradation-resistant PON1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that core fucosylation affects PON1 protein stability and resistance to degradation.

claim: Global and PON1-specific secretome de-N-glycosylation both limited the expansion of resistant clones in a tumor regression model.
source: Global and PON1-specific secretome de-N-glycosylation both limited the expansion of resistant clones in a tumor regression model.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tumor regression models showing that de-N-glycosylation prevents resistant clone expansion.

claim: Oxidative stress, inflammatory niche, and unfolded protein response are important factors for modulation by N-glycosylated TIS.
source: These genes characterize the oxidative stress, inflammatory niche, and unfolded protein response as important factors for this modulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome-wide analysis identifying genes related to oxidative stress, inflammation, and UPR as modulators of TIS response.

claim: Core fucosylation is a common modification indirectly induced by targeted therapies that paradoxically promotes resistance.
source: Our findings demonstrate that core fucosylation is a common modification indirectly induced by targeted therapies that paradoxically promotes resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive experimental data showing that targeted therapies induce core fucosylation which promotes drug resistance.

claim: Complete responses to targeted therapies remain rare for a vast majority of cancer patients.
source: Complete responses to targeted therapies remain rare for a vast majority of cancer patients (Krause and Van Etten, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature on targeted therapy outcomes.

claim: Resistance to targeted therapy is inevitable despite long-term disease stabilization achieved by therapeutic inhibition of oncogenic drivers.
source: While long-term disease stabilization can be achieved by therapeutic inhibition of oncogenic drivers, resistance to this targeted strategy is inevitable (Krause and Van Etten, 2005; Baselga, 2006; Lin and Shaw, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on targeted therapy resistance.

claim: Therapy-induced secretomes facilitate the selective expansion of pre-existing resistant clones.
source: For instance, a complex network of secreted signals from drug-stressed tumors termed therapy-induced secretomes (TIS) was shown to facilitate the selective expansion of a small number of pre-existing resistant clones, paradoxically explaining relapse to targeted therapy (Obenauf et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature on TIS and resistant clone expansion.

claim: Nearly all secreted mammalian proteins have at least one glycan attached to them at a specific site.
source: Glycosylation—the covalent addition of sugar moieties to target scaffolds—is the most abundant PTM of the secretome, as nearly all secreted mammalian proteins have at least one glycan, a sugar-based assembly, attached to them at a specific site (Spiro, 2002; Reily et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on protein glycosylation.

claim: FUT8 is the only enzyme-encoding gene known to directly mediate core fucosylation via N-linkages.
source: Of interest in terms of its consistent high pan-cancer expression profile in both data sets is FUT8—notably the only enzyme-encoding gene known to directly mediate core fucosylation via N-linkages (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature on FUT8 function.

claim: FUT8 broadly correlated with resistance to a variety of compounds but more strongly to inhibitors of receptor tyrosine kinase, epidermal growth factor receptor, and insulin-like growth factor receptor.
source: Indeed, FUT8 broadly correlated with resistance to a variety of compounds but more strongly to inhibitors of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK), epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and insulin-like growth factor receptor (IGFR).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacogenomics data analysis showing correlation between FUT8 expression and drug resistance.

claim: Cell lines that contain mutations near or specifically at GDP-Fuc binding sites in FUTs or other fucosylation genes collectively exhibited higher sensitivity to drugs.
source: Moreover, cell lines that contain mutations near or specifically at GDP-Fuc binding sites (resulting in amino acid change that eliminates or decreases fucosylation) in FUTs or other fucosylation genes collectively exhibited higher sensitivity to drugs (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of cell line mutations and drug sensitivity, with reference to figures showing the results.

claim: There is an extensive pan-cancer gene expression increase in both protein O- and N-linked glycosylation gene sets.
source: Similarly, there is an extensive pan-cancer gene expression increase in both groups (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cancer types exhibiting higher FUT methylation are more sensitive to targeted therapies with the exception of FUT1 and FUT6.
source: In other words, cancer types exhibiting higher FUT methylation are more sensitive to targeted therapies with the exception of FUT1 and FUT6 (Figure 1D), suggesting that cancer cells can inhibit fucosylation upon increased methylation of FUT promoter are more susceptible to therapy.
evidence: The claim is supported by methylation and drug sensitivity data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Lectin blotting revealed a distinct signature of enriched core fucosylation of serum proteins between 30 and 60 kDa in lung cancer patients who received multiple cycles of osimertinib, compared to those of treatment-naive patients.
source: Remarkably, lectin blotting revealed a distinct signature of enriched core fucosylation of serum proteins between 30 and 60 kDa in lung cancer (LC) patients who received multiple cycles of osimertinib, a third-generation EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), compared to those of treatment-naive patients (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by lectin blotting data from patient serum samples shown in figures.

claim: PNGase F-released N-glycans showed significantly higher levels in osimertinib-treated patients compared to treatment-naive patients.
source: Following analysis of in-gel excised 30~60 kDa patient serum proteins, PNGase F-released N-glycans showed significantly higher levels in osimertinib-treated patients compared to treatment-naive patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A), while this apparent difference was considerably moderated when N-glycans were released by either Endo S or F1.
evidence: The claim is supported by N-glycan release assay data from patient serum samples shown in figures.

claim: Targeted kinase inhibition by EGFR-TKIs, HER2-TKI, or BRAFi differentially induced fucosylation of secreted proteins <60 kDa.
source: Targeted kinase inhibition by EGFR-TKIs (gefitinib, erlotinib), HER2-TKI (lapatinib), or BRAFi (vemurafenib) differentially induced fucosylation of secreted proteins <60 kDa (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell culture experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Secretomes derived from drug-resistant clones displayed an induced <60 kDa protein fucosylation.
source: Similarly, secretomes derived from DR clones displayed an induced <60 kDa protein fucosylation (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from drug-resistant clone secretomes shown in Figure 1I.

claim: TIS derived from cancer cells treated with targeted inhibitors of EGFR, BRAF, or HER2 signaling unanimously led to an elevated secretome fucosylation.
source: TIS derived from cancer cells treated with targeted inhibitors of EGFR, BRAF, or HER2 signaling unanimously led to an elevated secretome fucosylation (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by sandwich ELLA measurements shown in Figure 1J.

claim: All drug-resistant clone-derived secretomes showed increased fucosylation compared to secretomes derived from parental clones.
source: Likewise, all DR clone-derived secretomes showed increased fucosylation compared to secretomes derived from parental clones (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by sandwich ELLA measurements shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Core fucosylation is accompanied by an overall increase in relapsed lung cancer patient tissues after sequential therapy and osimertinib-treated lung cancer patient sera.
source: These are further accompanied by an overall core fucosylation increase in relapsed LC patient tissues after sequential therapy and osimertinib-treated LC patient sera (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by sandwich ELLA measurements from patient samples shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Total core fucosylation discriminated between non-treated and osimertinib-treated lung cancer patient sera with an AUC of 0.961.
source: Total core fucosylation discriminated against the conditions with high sensitivity and specificity with the associated area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.961 and 0.915, respectively, based on sandwich ELLA measurements (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC curve analysis of sandwich ELLA data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Total core fucosylation discriminated between non-relapsed and relapsed lung cancer patient tissues with an AUC of 0.915.
source: Total core fucosylation discriminated against the conditions with high sensitivity and specificity with the associated area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.961 and 0.915, respectively, based on sandwich ELLA measurements (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC curve analysis of sandwich ELLA data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: High expression of the fucose salvage pathway, FUT8, and SLC35C1 are strongly correlated with relapse in breast cancer and lung cancer patients.
source: Gene expression and enzyme activity analysis revealed that high expression of the fucose salvage pathway, FUT8, and SLC35C1 are strongly correlated with relapse (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression and enzyme activity analysis from patient tissue samples shown in figures.

claim: There was an overall immediate increase (16 h post-treatment) in Golgi-localized core fucosylation in drug-stressed lung cancer and melanoma cells and sustained activation in their respective drug-resistant clones.
source: There was an overall immediate increase (16 h post-treatment) in Golgi-localized core fucosylation in drug-stressed LC and melanoma cells and sustained activation in their respective DR clones (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: There was a marked increase in FUT8 and SLC35C1 expression upon apoptosis-inducing targeted therapy in cancer cells with various oncogenic drivers.
source: While drug-induced expression changes varied between FUTs responsible for O- and N-linked glycosylation, there was a marked increase in FUT8 and SLC35C1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 8C), all of which are associated with apoptosis (3-day treatment; Figure 1—figure supplement 8D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in figures.

claim: In drug-resistant clones, both FUT8 and SLC35C1 expressions are amplified with a pronounced fucose salvage pathway.
source: In DR clones, both expressions are also amplified except with a pronounced fucose salvage pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data from drug-resistant clones shown in figures.

claim: FUT8 is not classified as an essential gene in both sensitive and resistant cancer cell lines.
source: FUT8 is not classified as an essential gene in both sensitive and resistant cancer cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 9A), despite marginally higher essentiality scores in TKI-resistant cells than sensitive cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of genome-wide RNAi screening data from the Cancer Dependency Map project shown in figures.

claim: Treatment with EGFR-TKI or BRAFi and selection for resistance both led to higher FUT8-dependent GDP-Fuc catalytic activity.
source: Regardless, treatment with EGFR-TKI or BRAFi and selection for resistance both led to higher FUT8-dependent GDP-Fuc catalytic activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GDP-Fuc activity assay data shown in figures.

claim: Non-lethal concentrations of nine kinase inhibitors induced FUT8 expression while near-lethal concentrations moderately mitigated this effect.
source: Non-lethal concentrations of nine kinase inhibitors induced FUT8 expression while near-lethal concentrations moderately mitigated this effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in figures.

claim: FUT8-targeting siRNAs augmented drug-induced cell killing and subsequent rescue was observed upon transfection with FUT8 cDNA.
source: FUT8-targeting siRNAs augmented drug-induced cell killing and subsequent rescue was observed upon transfection with FUT8 cDNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 9E), all independent of cell proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi and rescue experiment data shown in figures.

claim: AFP and A1AT displayed systemic elevation in lung cancer patient sera following osimertinib treatment and in secretomes of drug-stressed cells and drug-resistant clones.
source: Furthermore, well-known core fucosylated cancer biomarkers α-fetoprotein (AFP) and α–1-antitrypsin (A1AT), both >50 kDa, displayed systemic elevation in LC patient sera following osimertinib treatment and in secretomes of drug-stressed cells and DR clones, at least those expressing basal A1AT (Figure 1—figure supplement 10A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE analysis data from patient sera and cell secretomes shown in figures.

claim: Concentrated secreted proteins of >30 kDa from targeted inhibitor-treated cells, their respective drug-resistant clones, and EGFR-TKI-treated lung cancer patients display distinctively enriched core fucosylation and core α–1,6-linkages-containing N-glycans, but less so in >100 kDa pooled proteins.
source: Using molecular weight cut-off (MWCO) filtration, we confirmed that concentrated secreted proteins of >30 kDa from targeted inhibitor-treated cells, their respective DR clones, and EGFR-TKI-treated LC patients display distinctively enriched core fucosylation and core α–1,6-linkages-containing N-glycans, but less so in >100 kDa pooled proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 10C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MWCO filtration and fucosylation analysis data shown in figures.

claim: Core fucosylation can be controlled by FUT8 or SLC35C1 in vitro.
source: These can be controlled by FUT8 or SLC35C1, at least shown in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 10E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiment data shown in figures.

claim: Xenografted drug-resistant clones are resistant in vivo.
source: Aside from xenografted DR clones which are also resistant in vivo, residual parental tumors following EGFR-TKI therapy were also considered as 'resistant'.
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft experiment data showing drug resistance in vivo.

claim: An overall increase in serum fucosylation and a distinct signature of enriched core fucosylated serum proteins between 30 and 60 kDa was observed in EGFR-TKI-treated parental-xenografted mice compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: Using the same array of experiments to assay core fucosylation, we observed an overall increase in serum fucosylation and a distinct signature of enriched core fucosylated serum proteins between 30 and 60 kDa in EGFR-TKI-treated parental-xenografted mice compared to vehicle-treated mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 11B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fucosylation assay data from xenograft mouse sera shown in figures.

claim: EGFR-TKI therapy led to significant increase in PNGase-F-released N-glycans in parental-xenografted mice.
source: Following analysis of in-gel excised 30~60 kDa serum proteins, EGFR-TKI therapy led to significant increase in PNGase-F-released N-glycans in parental-xenografted mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 11D), while minimal to no significant differences where observed when N-glycans were released by either Endo S or F1.
evidence: The claim is supported by N-glycan release assay data from xenograft mouse sera shown in figures.

claim: >30 kDa serum proteins from EGFR-TKI-treated parental-xenografted mice display distinctively enriched core fucosylation and core fucose-containing N-glycans, but less so in >100 kDa pooled proteins.
source: Using MWCO filtration, we confirmed that these >30 kDa serum proteins from EGFR-TKI-treated parental-xenografted mice display distinctively enriched core fucosylation and core fucose-containing N-glycans (Figure 1—figure supplement 11E), but less so in >100 kDa pooled proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by MWCO filtration and fucosylation analysis data from xenograft mouse sera shown in figures.

claim: Drug-resistant clone-xenografted mice displayed an overall increase in serum core fucosylation and enrichment of core fucose-containing serum N-glycans compared to untreated parental-xenografted mice.
source: As expected, while DR clone-xenografted mice displayed an overall increase in serum core fucosylation and enrichment of core fucose-containing serum N-glycans compared to untreated parental-xenografted mice, EGFR-TKI therapy did not induce significant changes in the DR setting, at least in sera.
evidence: The claim is supported by fucosylation assay data from xenograft mouse sera.

claim: EGFR-TKI therapy did not induce significant changes in serum fucosylation in drug-resistant clone-xenografted mice.
source: As expected, while DR clone-xenografted mice displayed an overall increase in serum core fucosylation and enrichment of core fucose-containing serum N-glycans compared to untreated parental-xenografted mice, EGFR-TKI therapy did not induce significant changes in the DR setting, at least in sera.
evidence: The claim is supported by fucosylation assay data from xenograft mouse sera.

claim: Gene expression profiling showed variable FUT expressions but a unanimous marked increase in FUK-FPGT, FUT8, and SLC35C1 expressions associated with EGFR-TKI resistance in xenograft tumor tissues.
source: In xenograft tumor tissues, gene expression profiling showed variable FUT expressions but a unanimous marked increase in FUK-FPGT, FUT8, and SLC35C1 expressions associated with EGFR-TKI resistance (Figure 1—figure supplement 11F), reiterating the involvement of fucose salvage pathway in the systemic core fucosylation changes associated with TIS and EGFR-TKI resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data from xenograft tumor tissues shown in figures.

claim: Golgi-associated core and terminal fucosylation are both enriched in tumors of parental-xenografted and drug-resistant clone-xenografted mice following EGFR-TKI therapy.
source: Intriguingly, golgi-associated core and terminal fucosylation are both enriched in tumors of parental-xenografted and DR clone-xenografted mice following EGFR-TKI therapy (Figure 1—figure supplement 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from xenograft tumor tissues shown in figures.

claim: FUT8 or SLC35C1 can directly regulate the distinct <60 kDa secretome fucosylation specifically in drug-resistant clones but not in sensitive cells.
source: We reveal that FUT8 or SLC35C1 can directly regulate the distinct <60 kDa secretome fucosylation specifically in DR clones but not in sensitive cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential regulation of secretome fucosylation by FUT8 and SLC35C1 in resistant versus sensitive cells.

claim: >100 kDa secretome fucosylation can effectively be mediated by either FUT8 or SLC35C1 in sensitive cells.
source: We note that >100 kDa secretome fucosylation can effectively be mediated by either of the two factors in sensitive cells, uncovering differential target processing of core fucosylated products prior to their secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing regulation of >100 kDa secretome fucosylation by FUT8 and SLC35C1 in sensitive cells.

claim: Targeted therapies induce a prevalent pan-cancer secretome core fucosylation that is primarily regulated by the fucose salvage-SLC35C1-FUT8 pathway and is enriched in the Golgi prior to secretion.
source: Regardless, taken together, our results suggest that targeted therapies induce a prevalent pan-cancer secretome core fucosylation that is primarily regulated by the fucose salvage-SLC35C1-FUT8 pathway and is enriched in the Golgi prior to secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive experimental data from multiple model systems showing therapy-induced secretome fucosylation regulated by the fucose salvage-SLC35C1-FUT8 pathway.

claim: Therapy-induced secretome core fucosylation is an evolvable mechanism towards establishing resistance.
source: This therapy-induced modification presumably is an evolvable mechanism towards establishing resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing association between secretome fucosylation and drug resistance.

claim: The population of the admixed gefitinib-resistant clone gradually expanded while the sensitive cell population significantly decreased upon targeted therapy in 3D tumor spheroid admixtures.
source: Following the formation of a 3D tumor spheroid, the population of the admixed gefitinib-resistant (GR) clone gradually expanded (observable after day 1 and steady from day 5), while the sensitive cell population significantly decreased upon targeted therapy (Figure 2B and Videos 1 and 2; representative PC9 admixture in Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-imaging confocal microscopy data from 3D tumor spheroid admixtures shown in figures and videos.

claim: Addition of PNGase F to admixture secretomes led to a striking protein de-N-glycosylation in culture.
source: Addition of PNGase F to these admixture secretomes led to a striking protein de-N-glycosylation in culture (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by glycoprotein staining and sandwich ELLA data shown in figures.

claim: Therapy-induced regression of mostly sensitive cells and population expansion of admixed minority gefitinib-resistant and erlotinib-resistant clones are tightly linked with increased secretome core fucosylation.
source: Therefore, therapy-induced regression of mostly sensitive cells and population expansion of admixed minority GR and erlotinib-resistant (ER) clones are tightly linked with increased secretome core fucosylation (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by AAL blotting, sandwich ELLA, and N-glycan release assay data from cell admixtures shown in figures.

claim: Secretome de-N-glycosylation blocked the growth acceleration of the drug-resistant clone promoted by therapy-induced secretome in various cancer backgrounds and targeted therapy settings.
source: In both 3D and 2D admixture assays, secretome de-N-glycosylation blocked the growth acceleration of the DR clone promoted by TIS in various cancer backgrounds and targeted therapy settings (Figure 2F and G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), delayed the S-phase cycle of residual cell populations, and promoted apoptosis (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell tracking and cell cycle analysis data from admixture experiments shown in figures.

claim: Therapy-induced secretome stimulated the proliferation of low-density seeded drug-resistant clones while exposure to de-N-glycosylated therapy-induced secretome limited their outgrowth.
source: Consistently, in a CM co-culture assay, TIS stimulated the proliferation of low-density seeded DR clones while exposure to de-N-glycosylated TIS limited their outgrowth (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation assay data from conditioned media co-culture experiments shown in figures.

claim: De-N-glycosylation in fresh media or DMSO conditioned media did not affect drug-resistant clone proliferation.
source: Of note, de-N-glycosylation in fresh media or DMSO CM did not affect DR clone proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation assay data from conditioned media co-culture experiments shown in figures.

claim: Depletion of FUT8 or SLC35C1 efficiently blocked the expansion of drug-resistant clone population in a regressed cell admixture at day 5.
source: At day 5, depletion of FUT8 or SLC35C1 efficiently blocked the expansion of DR clone population in a regressed cell admixture (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), suggesting that the similar effect afforded by PNGase F is via protein de-N-glycosylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi and cell tracking data from admixture experiments shown in figures.

claim: Depletion of fucosylation and intracellular kinase phospho-proteome was observed in cell admixtures upon FUT8 or SLC35C1 depletion.
source: In such a circumstance, we observed depletion of fucosylation (in both apoptotic bodies and soluble secretome) and intracellular kinase phospho-proteome (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by sandwich ELLA and phospho-RTK array data from cell admixtures shown in figures.

claim: De-N-glycosylated therapy-induced secretome prevented drug-resistant clones to form colonies and decreased kinase phosphorylation activity of EGFR, MET, and ErbB3.
source: We corroborated these in a CM co-culture assay (Figure 2K), wherein de-N-glycosylated TIS prevented DR clones to form colonies and decreased kinase phosphorylation activity of EGFR, MET, and ErbB3, at least in GR and ER clones, respectively (Figure 2L and M).
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay and ELISA data from conditioned media co-culture experiments shown in figures.

claim: De-N-glycosylation by PNGase F in conditioned media co-cultures did not significantly influence the drug sensitivity of both sensitive cells and drug-resistant clones, except in sensitive cells cultured in their own de-N-glycosylated therapy-induced secretome where there is a widespread drug sensitization.
source: De-N-glycosylation by PNGase F in CM co-cultures (fresh media or CM from same cell/clone source) did not significantly influence the drug sensitivity of both sensitive cells and DR clones (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), except in sensitive cells cultured in their own de-N-glycosylated TIS, where there is a widespread drug sensitization (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by drug sensitivity assay data from conditioned media co-culture experiments shown in figures.

claim: Fucosylation of the therapy-induced secretome from drug-treated sensitive cells is critical to its survival-enhancing effects not only on drug-resistant clones but also in drug-sensitive cells.
source: These point to the idea that fucosylation of the TIS from drug-treated sensitive cells is critical to its survival-enhancing effects not only on DR clones but also in drug-sensitive cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from drug sensitivity assay data showing effects of de-N-glycosylated TIS on both resistant and sensitive cells.

claim: PNGase F in-culture for up to 5 days did not affect cell proliferation across all cell lines and drug-resistant clones.
source: Across all cell lines and DR clones, PNGase F in-culture for up to 5 days did not affect cell proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in figures.

claim: At day 5, there was only a significant increase in fucosylation from therapy-induced secretome and ER/Golgi fractions, not from cell membrane fractions, of EGFR-TKI-treated H1993 and PC9 admixtures.
source: At day 5, we only observed a significant increase in fucosylation from TIS and ER/Golgi fractions, not from cell membrane fractions, of EGFR-TKI-treated H1993 and PC9 admixtures (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sandwich ELLA data from subcellular fractionation experiments shown in figures.

claim: There were no changes in the <60 kDa fucosylation signature in cell membrane fractions of the admixtures, unlike the significant increase in ER/Golgi fraction.
source: In addition, there were no changes in the <60 kDa fucosylation signature in cell membrane fractions of the admixtures, unlike the significant increase in ER/Golgi fraction (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sandwich ELLA data from subcellular fractionation experiments shown in figures.

claim: PNGase F effectively de-N-glycosylated cell membrane proteins in-culture of both EGFR-TKI-treated H1993 and PC9 admixtures.
source: Regardless, PNGase F effectively de-N-glycosylated cell membrane proteins in-culture of both EGFR-TKI-treated H1993 and PC9 admixtures (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by glycoprotein staining and sandwich ELLA data from subcellular fractionation experiments shown in figures.

claim: Core fucosylation of the therapy-induced secretome, and not of membrane proteins, promotes the drug-resistant clone population expansion observed in cell admixture experiments.
source: Although we cannot completely rule out alternative possibilities, these results favor the idea that core fucosylation of the TIS, and not of membrane proteins, promotes the DR clone population expansion observed in our cell admixture experiments.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from subcellular fractionation and de-N-glycosylation experiments.

claim: Co-culture with EGFR-TKI-treated sensitive cells significantly promoted the growth of drug-resistant clones while the addition of PNGase F in the culture pronouncedly led to their growth retardation in 'sequentially layered' 3D spheroid co-cultures.
source: Resembling our initial findings, co-culture with EGFR-TKI (gefitinib or erlotinib)-treated sensitive cells significantly promoted the growth of DR clones while the addition of PNGase F in the culture pronouncedly led to their growth retardation (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data from 3D spheroid co-culture experiments shown in figures.

claim: Therapy-induced secretome de-N-glycosylation triggered the senescence-associated secretory phenotype and impeded the gene expression of factors previously described to promote resistant cell outgrowth in a regressing tumor microenvironment in 3D admixtures at day 5.
source: In these 3D admixtures at day 5, TIS de-N-glycosylation triggered the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) and impeded the gene expression of factors previously described to promote resistant cell outgrowth in a regressing TME (Obenauf et al., 2015; Figure 2N).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from 3D admixture experiments shown in figures, with citation to published literature.

claim: The response of drug-resistant clones in admixtures upon therapy-induced secretome de-N-glycosylation is independent of fucosylation gene activity.
source: It appears that the response of DR clones in these admixtures upon TIS de-N-glycosylation is independent of fucosylation gene activity since there were no marked changes in expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression data shown in figures.

claim: Long-term passaging and culture of drug-resistant clones in de-N-glycosylated therapy-induced secretome initiated a senescence response shown by strong SA-β-gal activity, SASP activation, and arrested growth.
source: Notably, long-term passaging and culture of DR clones in de-N-glycosylated TIS initiated a senescence response shown by strong senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity, SASP activation, and arrested growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), elucidating the inhibited proliferative capacity of these clones in cell admixtures upon TIS de-N-glycosylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by SA-β-gal staining, qPCR, and proliferation assay data shown in figures.

claim: The rebound of the drug-resistant clone population in a model of tumor regression is dependent on fucosylated scaffolds of the therapy-induced secretome.
source: These results demonstrate that the rebound of the DR clone population in a model of tumor regression is dependent on fucosylated scaffolds of the TIS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comprehensive experimental data showing effects of TIS de-N-glycosylation on resistant clone expansion.

claim: Label-free in-gel proteomics retrieved a fairly reproducible amount of peptide sequences per sample from AAL-captured 30~70 kDa secretome proteins.
source: Our analysis retrieved a fairly reproducible amount of peptide sequences per sample, which we used for downstream target identification (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in figures.

claim: Base peak chromatogram revealed differential mass ranges in all samples, with a relatively higher overlapping similarity between gefitinib-treated cells and gefitinib-resistant clone.
source: Base peak chromatogram revealed differential mass ranges in all samples, with a relatively higher overlapping similarity between gefitinib-treated cells and GR clone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in figures.

claim: The proteomics screen derived >60% 'contaminant' protein coverage from non-secreted apoptotic proteins, serum proteins, uncharacterized proteins, immunoglobulins, and proteins outside the target size range.
source: As expected, we derived >60% 'contaminant' protein coverage.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data analysis.

claim: After filtering contaminants, the proteomics screen yielded a total of 57 unique, secretory-predicted proteins across the three conditions.
source: We filtered these out and retained proteins that are only classified as 'secretory' or 'extracellular' based on the annotation criteria by UniProt (i.e. possession of N-terminal signal sequence), yielding a total of 57 unique, secretory-predicted proteins across the three conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data analysis with filtering based on UniProt annotation.

claim: Gene ontology analysis showed significant enrichment of biological processes implicated in stress response, secretory pathway, and protein maturation in the ER/Golgi.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis showed significant enrichment of biological processes (BPs) implicated in stress response, secretory pathway, and protein maturation in the ER/Golgi (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis of proteomics data shown in figures.

claim: Biological processes related to the metabolic regulation of oxidative stress were significantly overrepresented in the proteomics data.
source: Interestingly, BPs related to the metabolic regulation of oxidative stress were significantly overrepresented.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis of proteomics data.

claim: 11 top hits were identified as overlapping fucosylated secretome proteins between gefitinib-treated H1993 cells and gefitinib-resistant clone using two different quantitative approaches (LFQ and iBAQ).
source: Following the selection of overlapping fucosylated secretome proteins between the gefitinib-treated H1993 cells and GR clone, we identified 11 top hits using two different quantitative approaches (label-free quantification [LFQ] and intensity-based absolute quantification [iBAQ]).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data analysis.

claim: Many of the top proteomics hits are serum proteins described to have aberrant N-glycosylation during cancer progression, such as AFP and PDIA3.
source: Many of these hits are serum proteins described to have aberrant N-glycosylation during cancer progression, such as AFP (Pinho and Reis, 2015) and the protein disulfide isomerase PDIA3 (LaMantia et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data with citations to published literature on protein glycosylation in cancer.

claim: In the gefitinib-treated H1993 cell secretome, PON1 showed strong fucosylation with two isoforms: one with an apparent molecular mass of ~55 kDa and the other ~45 kDa.
source: In the gefitinib-treated H1993 cell secretome, we confirmed strong fucosylation of PON1, which appeared to have two isoforms: one with an apparent molecular mass of ~55 kDa while the other is ~45 kDa (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and AAL blot data shown in figures.

claim: There was a widespread elevation of fucosylated secretome PON1 levels in multiple cancer cells upon targeted therapy despite different cell lineages, different oncogenic drivers, and different drugs.
source: Despite different cell lineages, different oncogenic drivers, and different drugs, we found a widespread elevation of fucosylated secretome PON1 levels in multiple cancer cells upon targeted therapy (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE data from multiple cell lines shown in figures.

claim: PON1 fucosylation is enriched in secretomes derived from drug-resistant clones.
source: Similarly, PON1 fucosylation is enriched in secretomes derived from DR clones (at least those that have detectable PON1 gene expression) (Figure 3F) and is strikingly elevated in LC patient sera upon osimertinib treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE data from drug-resistant clone secretomes shown in figures.

claim: PON1 fucosylation is strikingly elevated in lung cancer patient sera upon osimertinib treatment.
source: Similarly, PON1 fucosylation is enriched in secretomes derived from DR clones (at least those that have detectable PON1 gene expression) (Figure 3F) and is strikingly elevated in LC patient sera upon osimertinib treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE and immunoblot data from patient sera shown in figures.

claim: The ~55 kDa isoform of secreted PON1 is favorably N-glycosylated than the ~45 kDa isoform, both of which have aberrantly high levels in osimertinib-treated patient sera.
source: Immunoprecipitated PON1 from core fucosylation-enriched patient sera reveals that the ~55 kDa isoform of secreted PON1 is favorably N-glycosylated than the ~45 kDa isoform, both of which have aberrantly high levels in osimertinib-treated patient sera (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and AAL blot data from patient sera shown in figures.

claim: PON1 fucosylation discriminated between non-treated and osimertinib-treated lung cancer patient sera with an AUC of 0.901.
source: PON1 fucosylation discriminated against the conditions with high sensitivity and specificity with the associated area under the curve (AUC) of 0.901, based on HLE measurements (Figure 3I, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC curve analysis of HLE data from patient sera shown in figures.

claim: Serum paraoxonase and arylesterase activities of PON1 were significantly differentiated between non-treated and osimertinib-treated lung cancer patient sera.
source: Supporting this idea, serum paraoxonase and arylesterase activities of PON1 were significantly differentiated between non-treated and osimertinib-treated LC patient sera (Figure 3I, right and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data from patient sera shown in figures.

claim: Serum paraoxonase and arylesterase activities significantly discriminated the treatment group with AUCs ranging from 0.76 to 0.89.
source: Also, both of these enzyme activities significantly discriminated the treatment group with AUCs ranging from 0.76 to 0.89.
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC curve analysis of enzyme activity data from patient sera.

claim: In lung cancer patient tissues, PON1 fucosylation is associated with relapse and discriminated it from non-relapsed lung cancer with an AUC of 0.77.
source: In LC patient tissues, PON1 fucosylation is associated with relapse and discriminated it from non-relapsed LC with an AUC of 0.77 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE data from patient tissues shown in figures.

claim: PON1 is primarily localized in the Golgi and has active fucosylation in the Golgi/ER fractions of gefitinib-resistant and vemurafenib-resistant clones.
source: PON1 is primarily localized in the Golgi and has active fucosylation in the Golgi/ER fractions of GR and vemurafenib-resistant (VR) clones (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and AAL blot data shown in figures.

claim: SLC35C1 RNAi significantly reduced Golgi-enriched PON1 fucosylation and promiscuously induced overall fucosylation in the nucleus of both drug-resistant clones.
source: SLC35C1 RNAi significantly reduced Golgi-enriched PON1 fucosylation and promiscuously induced overall fucosylation in the nucleus of both DR clones (Figure 3L and M), indicating a functional defect in the transport of GDP-Fuc along the secretory pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE and confocal microscopy data from RNAi experiments shown in figures.

claim: Among the top 20 PON1 co-expressing proteins, only PON3 and VWA7 showed co-localization with PON1 in the secretory pathway.
source: Among the top 20 proteins, only paraoxonase 3 (PON3) and VWA7 showed co-localization with PON1 in the secretory pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-expression analysis and protein localization data from CCLE.

claim: PON3 is a serum paraoxonase known to both preferentially interact and share numerous conserved PTM sites with PON1.
source: We were intrigued by PON3, also a serum paraoxonase known to both preferentially interact and share numerous conserved PTM (i.e. N-glycosylation) sites with PON1 (Harel et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature on PON3-PON1 interaction.

claim: There is an active co-localization between PON1 and PON3 in both gefitinib-resistant and vemurafenib-resistant clones.
source: In both GR and VR clones, there is an active co-localization between PON1 and PON3 (Figure 3O).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in figures.

claim: High PON3 expression correlated well with relapse in breast cancer patient tissues.
source: While PON1 expression did not discriminate non-relapsed and relapsed BC patient tissues, high PON3 expression correlated well with relapse (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and immunohistochemistry data from patient tissues shown in figures.

claim: PON3 expression is increased in various drug-stressed cells and drug-resistant clones.
source: In addition, PON3 expression is increased in various drug-stressed cells and DR clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in figures.

claim: In Golgi/ER of H1993-GR, both PON3 and SLC35C1 RNAi, but not PON1 RNAi, inhibited PON1 fucosylation.
source: In Golgi/ER of H1993-GR, both PON3 and SLC35C1 RNAi, but not PON1 RNAi, inhibited PON1 fucosylation (Figure 3P), demonstrating that PON3 directs PON1 fucosylation prior to secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE data from RNAi experiments shown in figures.

claim: Only PON1 RNAi, not PON3 or SLC35C1 RNAi, impeded Golgi/ER-specific paraoxonase activity.
source: Moreover, only PON1 RNAi, not PON3 or SLC35C1 RNAi, impeded Golgi/ER-specific paraoxonase activity (Figure 3P), reflecting known differences between the two PONs in hydrolyzing paraoxon (Draganov et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data from RNAi experiments shown in figures, with citation to published literature.

claim: PON3 or SLC35C1 RNAi could ablate FUT8-directed transfer of fucose moiety from GDP-Fuc to N-glycan GlcNAc residue of PON1 in a cross-linking GDP-Fuc activity assay.
source: In a cross-linking GDP-Fuc activity assay, we showed that PON3 or SLC35C1 RNAi could ablate FUT8-directed transfer of fucose moiety from GDP-Fuc to N-glycan GlcNAc residue of PON1 (Figure 3Q), implying direct functional regulation of PON1 fucosylation by PON3.
evidence: The claim is supported by GDP-Fuc activity assay data from RNAi experiments shown in figures.

claim: In the secretome, PON1 is de-N-glycosylated upon exogenous addition of PNGase F onto cultures of sensitive cells and drug-resistant clones but without marked changes in GDP-Fuc activity on PON1 in Golgi/ER or PON1 secretion.
source: Confirming the depletion of secretome PON1 fucosylation by a glycosidase, we showed that in the secretome, PON1 is de-N-glycosylated upon exogenous addition of PNGase F onto cultures of sensitive cells and DR clones but without marked changes in GDP-Fuc activity on PON1 in Golgi/ER or PON1 secretion in sensitive cells, DR clones, and cells engineered to overexpress PON1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE, GDP-Fuc activity assay, and ELISA data shown in figures.

claim: EGFR-TKI-induced or EGFR-TKI resistance-associated abundance of PON1-interacting PON3 in whole cell lysates, golgi fractions, and secretomes are all linked with increased PON1 core fucosylation and PON1-bound core N-glycan enrichment.
source: Hinted by its strong co-expression with PON1 and functional implication on PON1 core fucosylation, EGFR-TKI-induced or EGFR-TKI resistance-associated abundance of PON1-interacting PON3 in whole cell lysates, golgi fractions, and secretomes are all linked with increased PON1 core fucosylation and PON1-bound core N-glycan enrichment (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-linking coimmunoprecipitation and HLE data shown in figures.

claim: Similar signatures of increased PON1 core fucosylation and PON1-bound N-glycans were observed with PON1-interacting VWF in golgi fractions and secretomes of EGFR-TKI-treated cells and drug-resistant clones.
source: Similar signatures were observed with PON1-interacting VWF (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C), at least in golgi fractions and secretomes of EGFR-TKI-treated cells and DR clones.
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-linking coimmunoprecipitation and HLE data shown in figures.

claim: MPO is associated with decreased PON1 interaction, decreased core fucosylation, and lesser PON1-bound N-glycans across EGFR-TKI-treated cells and drug-resistant clones.
source: In contrast, MPO is associated with decreased PON1 interaction, decreased core fucosylation, and lesser PON1-bound N-glycans across EGFR-TKI-treated cells and DR clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-linking coimmunoprecipitation and HLE data shown in figures.

claim: Transcriptional control of both PON1 and PON3 by SREBP2 tightly regulate PON1-PON3 interaction and PON3-mediated PON1 core fucosylation in the golgi and secretomes of EGFR-TKI-treated cells and drug-resistant clones.
source: In addition, transcriptional control of both PON1 and PON3 by SREBP2, a master transcription factor (TF) for PON promoter activity, tightly regulate PON1-PON3 interaction and PON3-mediated PON1 core fucosylation in the golgi and secretomes of EGFR-TKI-treated cells and DR clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi, qPCR, and HLE data shown in figures.

claim: PON3's regulatory effect on PON1 core fucosylation is dependent on its direct binding with PON1 and its effects on PON1 enzyme activity.
source: These data suggest that PON3's regulatory effect on PON1 core fucosylation is dependent on its direct binding with PON1 and its effects on PON1 enzyme activity, and that direct control of PON3 is sufficient to regulate PON1 core fucosylation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cross-linking coimmunoprecipitation and functional assay data.

claim: Direct control of PON3 is sufficient to regulate PON1 core fucosylation.
source: These data suggest that PON3's regulatory effect on PON1 core fucosylation is dependent on its direct binding with PON1 and its effects on PON1 enzyme activity, and that direct control of PON3 is sufficient to regulate PON1 core fucosylation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from RNAi and functional assay data.

claim: Core fucosylated PON1 is a major component of the constitutive N-glycome of the cancer therapy-induced secretome and a signature of targeted therapy resistance.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that core fucosylated PON1 is a major component of the constitutive N-glycome of the cancer TIS and a signature of targeted therapy resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comprehensive experimental data showing PON1 fucosylation in TIS and its association with drug resistance.

claim: PON1 has 23 predicted N-glycosylation sites with four Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons all scored above the 'high potential' threshold.
source: PON1 has 23 predicted N-glycosylation sites with four Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons–consensus amino acid sequences that determine N-glycosylation efficiency–all scored above the 'high potential' threshold (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by N-glycosylation site prediction analysis shown in figures.

claim: PON1 is predicted to be mostly folded and has a negative net electrical charge (–16 at pH 7).
source: PON1 is predicted to be mostly folded and has a negative net electrical charge (–16 at pH 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein folding and charge prediction analysis.

claim: All four sequons of PON1 (N227, N253, N270, N324) and their immediate vicinity have either neutral (0) or negative (ranging from –0.4––0.2) net charge.
source: All four sequons of PON1 (N227, N253, N270, N324) and their immediate vicinity have either neutral (0) or negative (ranging from –0.4––0.2) net charge (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by charge prediction analysis shown in figures.

claim: Among the four sequons, N324(GT) and N270(IS) are well conserved throughout species while N253(WT) is uniquely conserved in mammals.
source: Among the four sequons, N324(GT) and N270(IS) are well conserved throughout species while N253(WT) is uniquely conserved in mammals (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in figures.

claim: Both N253(WT) and N324(GT) sequons are located in the outer region of PON1's β-propeller structure while the other sequons are found in the innermost tunnel structure near the calcium-binding sites.
source: Both N253(WT) and N324(GT) sequons are located in the outer region of PON1's β-propeller structure while the other sequons are found in the innermost tunnel structure near the calcium-binding sites (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein structure analysis shown in figures.

claim: Six aberrantly fucosylated glycans were determined to be released from immunoprecipitated PON1, where GlcNAc2Man3 + HexNAc2Fuc1 putative glycan structures are commonly present.
source: We determined six aberrantly fucosylated glycans released from immunoprecipitated PON1, where GlcNAc2Man3 + HexNAc2Fuc1 putative glycan structures are commonly present (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by tandem mass spectrometry data shown in figures.

claim: Two of the most abundant glycans (peaks 1 and 2) were identified to have high FUT8 substrate specificity, while the rest (peaks 3–6) have either low specificity or not yet identified.
source: Two of the most abundant glycans (peaks 1 and 2) were identified to have high FUT8 substrate specificity, while the rest (peaks 3–6) have either low specificity or not yet identified (Figure 4E, bottom; García-García et al., 2020; Tseng et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by tandem mass spectrometry data shown in figures, with citations to published literature on FUT8 substrate specificity.

claim: Both PON1 mutants (N253G and N324G) selectively reduced PON1 core fucosylation and prevented efficient GDP-Fuc transfer.
source: Both PON1 mutants selectively reduced PON1 core fucosylation and prevented efficient GDP-Fuc transfer (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by AAL blot, HLE, and GDP-Fuc activity assay data from site-directed mutagenesis experiments shown in figures.

claim: N253G displayed more robust effects than N324G in reducing PON1 core fucosylation.
source: Note that N253G displayed more robust effects than N324G.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from site-directed mutagenesis experiments.

claim: PON1 mutants only had subtle effects on overall secretome N-glycosylation and did not alter gene expression of PON1, PON3, fucose salvage factors, GDP-fucose transporter, and fucosylatransferase.
source: These mutants only had subtle effects on overall secretome N-glycosylation and did not alter gene expression of PON1, PON3, fucose salvage factors (FUK, GMD), GDP-fucose transporter (SLC35C1), and fucosylatransferase (FUT8) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and glycoprotein staining data from site-directed mutagenesis experiments shown in figures.

claim: Wild-type or PON1 mutants did not have significant effects on the response of sensitive cells to EGFR-TKIs while both N253G and N324G mutants sensitized both gefitinib-resistant and erlotinib-resistant clones to EGFR inhibition.
source: WT or PON1 mutants did not have significant effects on the response of sensitive cells to EGFR-TKIs while both N253G and N324G mutants, not FL, sensitized both GR and ER clones to EGFR inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that PON1 fucosylation is a resistance selected mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by drug sensitivity assay data from site-directed mutagenesis experiments shown in figures.

claim: N253G remarkably promoted PON1 misfolding by completely sensitizing PON1 to cleavage by trypsin in whole gefitinib-resistant clone lysates.
source: Immunoblotting of whole GR clone lysates revealed that N253G remarkably promoted PON1 misfolding by completely sensitizing PON1 to cleavage by trypsin.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data from trypsin sensitivity assay.

claim: N324G induced a noticeable PON1 cleavage only at a higher trypsin concentration.
source: N324G induced a noticeable PON1 cleavage only at a higher trypsin concentration (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data from trypsin sensitivity assay shown in figures.

claim: In the Golgi/ER of gefitinib-resistant clone, similar effects were afforded on PON1 by N253G and N324G mutations when tested using ELISA and on protein glycosylation after PON1 immunoprecipitation.
source: In the Golgi/ER of GR clone, similar effects were also afforded on PON1 when tested using ELISA and on protein glycosylation after PON1 immunoprecipitation (Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA and glycoprotein staining data from trypsin sensitivity assay shown in figures.

claim: In Golgi/ER of A549 cells, N253G did not alter PON1's sensitivity to trypsin.
source: In Golgi/ER of A549 cells, where there is basal PON1 expression, N253G did not alter PON1's sensitivity to trypsin.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data from trypsin sensitivity assay.

claim: The same N253G mutation rendered PON1 from PON1-overexpressing cells sensitized to trypsin.
source: Conversely, the same mutation rendered PON1 from PON1-overexpressing cells sensitized to trypsin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data from trypsin sensitivity assay shown in figures.

claim: EGFR-TKI resistance or PON1 overexpression delayed the degradation of nascent polypeptides upon cycloheximide treatment.
source: Furthermore, EGFR-TKI resistance or PON1 overexpression delayed the degradation of nascent polypeptides upon CHX treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by EZClick labeling analysis data from cycloheximide chase assay shown in figures.

claim: In the gefitinib-resistant clone, N253G had no significant effect on overall protein synthesis.
source: In the GR clone, N253G had no significant effect on overall protein synthesis (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by EZClick labeling analysis data shown in figures.

claim: EGFR-TKI resistance delayed the degradation of total fucosylated proteins and Golgi-specific PON1-immunoprecipitated glycoproteins.
source: In addition, EGFR-TKI resistance delayed the degradation of total fucosylated proteins and Golgi-specific PON1-immunoprecipitated glycoproteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Coomassie staining and glycoprotein staining data from cycloheximide chase assay shown in figures.

claim: In the gefitinib-resistant clone, N253G accelerated the degradation of the lower kDa isoform of PON1, presumably its fucosylated form.
source: In the GR clone, N253G accelerated the degradation of the lower kDa isoform of PON1, presumably its fucosylated form (Figure 4L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data from cycloheximide chase assay shown in figures.

claim: N253G significantly ablated PON1 secretion while N324G displayed a modest effect.
source: More importantly, N253G significantly ablated PON1 secretion while N324G displayed a modest effect (Figure 4M).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data from secretome analysis shown in figures.

claim: N253G inhibited the intracellular arylesterase, but not paraoxonase, activity in gefitinib-resistant clone.
source: Unexpectedly, N253G inhibited the intracellular arylesterase, but not paraoxonase, activity in GR clone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in figures.

claim: N-glycosylation of PON1 governs its enzyme activity.
source: This is consistent with our hypothesis that N-glycosylation of PON1 governs its enzyme activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from enzyme activity assay data showing effects of N253G mutation on PON1 enzyme activity.

claim: Core fucosylation promotes PON1 stability prior to secretion in drug-resistant clones and PON1-overexpressing cells.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that core fucosylation promotes PON1 stability prior to secretion in DR clones and PON1-overexpressing cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comprehensive experimental data showing effects of core fucosylation on PON1 stability and secretion.

claim: Fucosylation affords a more stable, degradation-resistant PON1 state in the secretion, which involves a rewired enzyme activity.
source: This offers an answer to our long-standing question of how fucosylation affords a more stable, degradation-resistant PON1 state in the secretion, which seems to involve a rewired enzyme activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comprehensive experimental data showing effects of fucosylation on PON1 stability and enzyme activity.

claim: Inhibition of PON1 core fucosylation via PON3 silencing or PON1-N253G mutation in sensitive cells significantly prevented the population expansion of drug-resistant clones in regressed cell admixtures at day 5.
source: Inhibition of PON1 core fucosylation via PON3 silencing or PON1-N253G mutation in sensitive cells significantly prevented the population expansion of DR clones in regressed cell admixtures at day 5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE and cell tracking data from admixture experiments shown in figures.

claim: PON1-N253G markedly sensitized EGFR-TKI-resistant tumors in mice without observable weight loss.
source: More importantly, PON1-N253G markedly sensitized EGFR-TKI-resistant tumors in mice without observable weight loss (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B), and led to systemic decrease of both EGFR-TKI-induced serum PON1 core fucosylation and PON1-bound N-glycans in xenografted mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft tumor growth and body weight data shown in figures.

claim: PON1-N253G led to systemic decrease of both EGFR-TKI-induced serum PON1 core fucosylation and PON1-bound N-glycans in xenografted mice.
source: More importantly, PON1-N253G markedly sensitized EGFR-TKI-resistant tumors in mice without observable weight loss (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and B), and led to systemic decrease of both EGFR-TKI-induced serum PON1 core fucosylation and PON1-bound N-glycans in xenografted mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by HLE and N-glycan release assay data from xenograft mouse sera shown in figures.

claim: PON1 core fucosylation is a critical and functional component of the cancer therapy-induced secretome that promotes targeted therapy resistance.
source: Collectively, these consistently support our hypothesis that PON1 core fucosylation is a critical and functional component of the cancer TIS that promotes targeted therapy resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comprehensive experimental data showing effects of PON1 core fucosylation on drug resistance.

claim: In a retrieved fraction of gefitinib-resistant clone upon therapy-induced secretome de-N-glycosylation in 2D admixture, ER stress (ATF6), amino acid response (AAR element; ATF2, ATF3, ATF4), androgen receptor (AR) pathways, and E2F transcription were distinctively up-regulated.
source: In a retrieved fraction of GR clone upon TIS de-N-glycosylation in 2D admixture, ER stress (ATF6), amino acid response (AAR element; ATF2, ATF3, ATF4), androgen receptor (AR) pathways, and E2F transcription were distinctively up-regulated, while stem cell factors (SOX2, NANOG, OCT4), interferon-stimulated response (ISR element; STAT1, STAT2), STAT3, and hypoxia (HIF) signaling were selectively repressed (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcription factor reporter array data from admixture experiments shown in figures.

claim: Stem cell factors (SOX2, NANOG, OCT4), interferon-stimulated response (ISR element; STAT1, STAT2), STAT3, and hypoxia (HIF) signaling were selectively repressed in gefitinib-resistant clone upon therapy-induced secretome de-N-glycosylation in 2D admixture.
source: In a retrieved fraction of GR clone upon TIS de-N-glycosylation in 2D admixture, ER stress (ATF6), amino acid response (AAR element; ATF2, ATF3, ATF4), androgen receptor (AR) pathways, and E2F transcription were distinctively up-regulated, while stem cell factors (SOX2, NANOG, OCT4), interferon-stimulated response (ISR element; STAT1, STAT2), STAT3, and hypoxia (HIF) signaling were selectively repressed (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcription factor reporter array data from admixture experiments shown in figures.

claim: In 3D admixtures of drug-resistant clone and sensitive cells, PON1-N253G transfection in sensitive cells phenocopied the effects of therapy-induced secretome de-N-glycosylation on intracellular signaling, senescence, regressing tumor microenvironment cues, kinase phospho-proteome, and growth of gefitinib-resistant and erlotinib-resistant clones.
source: In these admixtures, PON1-N253G transfection in sensitive cells phenocopied the effects of TIS de-N-glycosylation on intracellular signaling, senescence, regressing TME cues, kinase phospho-proteome, and growth of GR and ER clones (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR, confocal microscopy, phospho-RTK array, and cell tracking data from admixture experiments shown in figures.

claim: A cascade of ER stress and UPR-regulated translational reprogramming events mediate the blocking of drug-resistant clone growth upon therapy-induced secretome de-N-glycosylation or fucosylated PON1 inhibition.
source: These data point to a cascade of ER stress and UPR-regulated translational reprogramming events as mediators in blocking the growth of DR clones upon TIS de-N-glycosylation or fucosylated PON1 inhibition.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from transcription factor reporter array and gene expression data.

claim: Both therapy-induced secretome de-N-glycosylation and fucosylated PON1 inhibition actively induced Golgi/ER-localized ATF6 with enriched co-localization with fucosylated scaffold residues in drug-resistant clones.
source: In a CM co-culture, both TIS de-N-glycosylation and fucosylated PON1 inhibition actively induced Golgi/ER-localized ATF6 with enriched co-localization with fucosylated scaffold residues in DR clones (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and H), which probably implicates ER stress-induced translocation/sorting of ATF6 from ER to Golgi.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and ELISA data from conditioned media co-culture experiments shown in figures.

claim: De-N-glycosylating therapy-induced secretome and inhibiting therapy-induced secretome-specific fucosylated PON1 in regressing cell admixtures markedly stimulated the production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species.
source: Indeed, de-N-glycosylating TIS and inhibiting TIS-specific fucosylated PON1 in regressing cell admixtures markedly stimulated the production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS), a hallmark of redox imbalance (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROS/RNS detection assay data from admixture experiments shown in figures.

claim: In drug-resistant clones co-cultured in modified therapy-induced secretome with scarce PON1 fucosylation, silencing ATF6 prohibited the generation of intracellular ROS/RNS.
source: In DR clones co-cultured in modified TIS with scarce PON1 fucosylation, silencing ATF6 prohibited the generation of intracellular ROS/RNS (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROS/RNS detection assay data from RNAi experiments shown in figures.

claim: In gefitinib-treated 3D cell admixtures, PON1-N253G-bearing sensitive cells restrained the growth of gefitinib-resistant clone while ATF6 RNAi reverted this effect.
source: In gefitinib-treated 3D cell admixtures, PON1-N253G-bearing sensitive cells restrained the growth of GR clone while ATF6 RNAi reverted this effect (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell tracking data from admixture experiments shown in figures.

claim: PON1-N253G promoted a pro-inflammatory environment in cell admixtures with increased levels of IL-6, TNF-α, and GM-CSF cytokines in the secretome while ATF6 RNAi antagonized this induced cytokine signature.
source: PON1-N253G promoted a pro-inflammatory environment in the same cell admixtures with increased levels of IL-6, TNF-α, and GM-CSF cytokines in the secretome while ATF6 RNAi antagonized this induced cytokine signature (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by sandwich ELISA data from admixture experiments shown in figures.

claim: De-N-glycosylation of the therapy-induced secretome or inhibition of therapy-induced secretome-specific fucosylated PON1 markedly induced ATF3 and ATF4 in drug-resistant clones but this effect is negligible in the golgi.
source: Meanwhile, de-N-glycosylation of the TIS or inhibition of TIS-specific fucosylated PON1 markedly induced ATF3 and ATF4—both of which contain an amino acid response element (AARE) in their promoters (Ron and Walter, 2007) which was one of the hits identified from our TF screen (Figure 5A)—in DR clones but this effect is negligible in the golgi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data from conditioned media co-culture experiments shown in figures, with citation to published literature.

claim: Silencing ATF3 or ATF4 decreased intracellular ROS/RNS levels in drug-resistant clones co-cultured in modified therapy-induced secretome where fucosylated PON1 is inhibited.
source: Regardless, silencing ATF3 or ATF4 decreased intracellular ROS/RNS levels in DR clones co-cultured in modified TIS where fucosylated PON1 is inhibited (Figure 5—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROS/RNS detection assay data from RNAi experiments shown in figures.

claim: Localization-specific effects of ATF6, ATF3, ATF4 can be explained by differences in their retention and translocation in ER-golgi.
source: These localization-specific effects of ATF6, ATF3, ATF4 can likely be explained by differences in their retention and translocation in ER-golgi (Ron and Walter, 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data with citation to published literature on ATF protein localization.

claim: When overexpressed at a high degree (>700 fold) in cells without detectable PON1, there was an active PON1 fucosylation in the secretion.
source: When overexpressed at a high degree (>700 fold) in cells without detectable PON1 (H460 and H1993), we observed an active PON1 fucosylation in the secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PON1 overexpression experiments.

claim: Stably knocking-out PON1 in wild-type PON1-expressing cells did not alter PON1 fucosylation intracellularly or in the secretion.
source: Stably knocking-out PON1 in wild-type PON1-expressing cells (A549) did not alter PON1 fucosylation intracellularly or in the secretion while stably knocking-out SLC35C1 in PON1-overexpressing cells led to suppression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PON1 knockout experiments.

claim: Stably knocking-out SLC35C1 in PON1-overexpressing cells led to suppression of PON1 fucosylation.
source: Stably knocking-out PON1 in wild-type PON1-expressing cells (A549) did not alter PON1 fucosylation intracellularly or in the secretion while stably knocking-out SLC35C1 in PON1-overexpressing cells led to suppression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from SLC35C1 knockout experiments.

claim: Transfection of PON1-N253G construct or exogenous PNGase F treatment in PON1-overexpressing cells mitigated secretome PON1 fucosylation.
source: Additionally, transfection of PON1-N253G construct or exogenous PNGase F treatment in PON1-overexpressing cells mitigated secretome PON1 fucosylation (summary in Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from site-directed mutagenesis and PNGase F treatment experiments shown in figures.

claim: Modified cells with de-N-glycosylated secretome PON1 have increased ROS/RNS and a more pro-inflammatory secretome.
source: Accordingly, modified cells with de-N-glycosylated secretome PON1 have increased ROS/RNS and a more pro-inflammatory secretome (Figure 5K and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROS/RNS detection and sandwich ELISA data shown in figures.

claim: PON1 fucosylation-enriched therapy-induced secretome amplified the growth of gefitinib-resistant and erlotinib-resistant clones while cells with de-N-glycosylated PON1 prevented this growth coupled with increased intracellular caspase activities.
source: More importantly, PON1 fucosylation-enriched TIS amplified the growth of GR and ER clones while cells with de-N-glycosylated PON1 prevented this growth coupled with increased intracellular caspase activities (Figure 5M and N).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell tracking and caspase activity assay data shown in figures.

claim: UPR target genes were consistently up-regulated in drug-resistant clones co-cultured with therapy-induced secretome or PON1-overexpressing cell secretomes with de-N-glycosylated PON1.
source: Furthermore, UPR target genes were consistently up-regulated in DR clones co-cultured with TIS or PON1-overexpressing cell secretomes with de-N-glycosylated PON1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from conditioned media co-culture experiments shown in figures.

claim: In drug-resistant clones, restricted growth is associated with nuclear translocation of XBP1.
source: In the same DR clones, restricted growth is associated with nuclear translocation of XBP1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1N), indicating ATF6-induced transcription factor activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in figures.

claim: Similarity in gene expression profiles was observed in replicate samples and among conditions that represent control, positive fucosylation regulation, or negative PON1 fucosylation regulation in transcriptome-wide analysis.
source: The similarity in gene expression profiles was observed in replicate samples and among conditions that represent control (H1993 and H460), positive fucosylation regulation (gefitinib-treated H1993 and H460-PON1), or negative PON1 fucosylation regulation (PNGase-treated and PON1-N253G-transfected H460-PON1; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in figures.

claim: Secretome de-N-glycosylation and PON1 fucosylation inhibition led to 433 altered gene expression, and pathway analysis revealed that overlapped genes were enriched for negative regulators of the cell cycle and regulators of transcription and metabolism.
source: Secretome de-N-glycosylation and PON1 fucosylation inhibition led to 433 altered gene expression, and pathway analysis revealed that overlapped genes were enriched for negative regulators of the cell cycle and regulators of transcription and metabolism (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and GO analysis shown in figures.

claim: Secretome de-N-glycosylation and PON1 fucosylation inhibition generated a more down-regulated drug-resistant clone transcriptome associated with the regulation of receptor signaling pathways, cell communication, and cell proliferation.
source: The same conditions generated a more down-regulated DR clone transcriptome associated with the regulation of receptor signaling pathways, cell communication, and cell proliferation, among others (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and GO analysis shown in figures.

claim: Enriched secretome fucosylation led to fewer differentially expressed genes that are mostly involved in cellular metabolic reactions.
source: Enriched secretome fucosylation led to fewer differentially expressed genes that are mostly involved in cellular metabolic reactions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and GO analysis shown in figures.

claim: Only one overlapping altered gene was detected between the two conditions promoting secretome fucosylation (gefitinib treatment and PON1 overexpression).
source: Only one overlapping altered gene was detected between the two conditions promoting secretome fucosylation (gefitinib treatment and PON1 overexpression; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in figures.

claim: Secretome de-N-glycosylation led to 135 down- and 65 up-regulated genes, and secretome PON1 fucosylation inhibition resulted in 150 down- and 83 up-regulated genes, all with statistically significant p values.
source: Secretome de-N-glycosylation led to 135 down- and 65 up-regulated genes, and secretome PON1 fucosylation inhibition resulted in 150 down- and 83 up-regulated genes, all with statistically significant p values (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in figures.

claim: 21 genes were up-regulated while 90 genes were down-regulated in both secretome de-N-glycosylation and PON1 fucosylation inhibition conditions.
source: 21 genes were up-regulated while 90 genes were down-regulated in both conditions (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in figures.

claim: C19orf25, RPS27L, CLDN2, PAQR3, and SOX4 are putative blockers of secretome PON1 fucosylation-mediated drug-resistant clone outgrowth.
source: This analysis highlighted C19orf25, RPS27L, CLDN2, PAQR3, and SOX4 as putative blockers; while THBS1, F3, TAGLN, ANKRD1, and DKK1 as positive regulators of secretome PON1 fucosylation-mediated DR clone outgrowth (Figure 6E), all of which were validated in a separate gene expression analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and qPCR validation shown in figures.
